title: β2-Adrenoreceptor is a regulator of the α-synuclein gene driving risk of Parkinson's disease
authors: Mittal S, Bjørnevik K, Im DS, Flierl A, Dong X, Locascio JJ, et al.
followUp: 11 years (2004 to 2014) in the Norwegian Prescription Database
population: Screen of 1126 compounds in human SK-N-MC neuroblastoma cells; rat primary cortical neurons; mice; neuronal precursor cells from a patient with SNCA triplication; the Norwegian population alive on 1 January 2004 (4.6 million)
funder: Michael J. Fox Foundation; US National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (U01 NS082157, U01NS095736, R01 NS083845); US Department of Defense; M.E.M.O. Hoffman Foundation; Prinses Beatrix Spier Fonds; American Parkinson's Disease Association; Parkinson's Disease Foundation; Branfman Family Foundation; Canadian Institutes of Health Research; Brain Canada/Krembil Foundation; Heart and Stroke Foundation of Canada; Multiple System Atrophy Coalition; Harvard NeuroDiscovery Center.
authorConflicts: One author has applied for a related US patent; another is named inventor on a patent application relating to beta-adrenoreceptor agonists as potential Parkinson's disease therapeutics.
result: Cells: three beta2 agonists (metaproterenol, clenbuterol, salbutamol) lowered SNCA mRNA and alpha-synuclein protein in human neuroblastoma cells and rat neurons; beta2 knockout, silencing or propranolol raised them, and the effect tracked H3K27 acetylation at the SNCA promoter and enhancers. Mice: clenbuterol lowered nigral SNCA expression and protected dopaminergic neurons from MPTP. People: in Norway, salbutamol use was associated with a lower rate of Parkinson's disease (rate ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.76), adjusted for sex, age and education, and propranolol with a higher rate (2.20, 1.62 to 3.00). Inhaled corticosteroid use was not associated (0.95, 0.80 to 1.12), which the authors cite against confounding by smoking.
